messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kwame is a 33-year-old married man who came to treatment months after returning to the United States from a relief deployment in a war zone, where he had been responsible for documenting conditions and coordinating public updates for aid operations. During one attack on a distribution site, what had begun as a routine morning of photographing supply lines and sending messages to partner organizations turned chaotic within seconds. He remembers the sharp crack of gunfire, the crowd breaking apart, and the sickening realization that there was nowhere clearly safe to run. He had dropped behind a low wall with his phone still in his hand, trying to make sense of shouted instructions he could barely hear over the noise. What stayed with him most was not only the danger itself but the aftermath: civilians injured, colleagues shaken, and later the unbearable knowledge that those responsible would simply disappear back into the wider conflict without consequence. Since then, he has been unable to shake the conviction that what happened was profoundly unjust, that no one has been held accountable, and that in the one moment he most needed to act decisively, he cannot trust himself to know what to do.

These beliefs have hardened rather than softened since he came home. Kwame speaks about the attack with a restrained, flat quality at first, but underneath is a persistent sense of grievance and personal doubt. He has come to believe that the world is organized around impunity, that terrible things happen and nobody answers for them, and that this leaves him exposed in a way other people do not seem to understand. At the same time, he is certain he failed some inner test of competence; even though he survived, he sees his confusion during the attack as proof that he cannot rely on his own judgment when it matters. Those conclusions keep his body keyed up. He startles violently at sudden noises, struggles to settle even in ordinary environments, and finds himself perpetually on guard, as if his mind is trying to compensate for the danger and uncertainty he now expects everywhere.

That sense of threat follows him into his work as a social media manager, where he spends much of the day in a busy open-plan office with phones chiming, coworkers moving behind him, and video clips autoplaying on his screen. He catches himself scanning the room before he can focus on a campaign calendar, noticing exits, tracking who has entered, and reacting to any abrupt sound with a jolt that leaves him embarrassed. His concentration has deteriorated enough that tasks that once took minutes now stretch across an hour because his attention keeps shifting outward, checking for signs that something is wrong. In meetings he often sits where he can see the door. He tells himself this watchfulness is necessary because he cannot count on himself to respond well if something happens again.

Because feeling so on edge is exhausting, Kwame has developed ways of trying not to engage with anything that might pull him back toward the attack. When images or fragments of that day begin to surface, he pushes them away quickly and tries to detach from them, almost as if the memories belong to someone else. He avoids thinking about the event whenever he can, cutting off conversations with his wife if she asks how he is doing and redirecting himself into work metrics, scheduling, or scrolling. Yet even while he is trying not to think, he is checking windows, doorways, sounds in the hallway, and subtle shifts in other people’s expressions. His attempts to manage the fear have narrowed his life into a pattern of mental withdrawal and physical surveillance.

Over time, those habits have kept the danger feeling immediate. The more he detaches from the memories, the less processed they feel to him; they return as sharp, unfinished impressions that leave him tense and easily startled. The more he avoids thinking about what happened, the less able he feels to place it in the past, and his mind remains busy anticipating what could go wrong next. Constantly scanning his surroundings prevents any real sense of safety from taking hold. Even at home with his wife, a dropped utensil in the kitchen or a slammed car door outside can make him jump before he has time to think. She has noticed that he is present physically but often distant, and arguments have grown around his insistence on sitting facing restaurant entrances or leaving crowded places early.

What finally brought Kwame to seek help was a recent incident at work when a loud crash from a delivery cart in the hallway made him jerk upright, heart pounding, unable to refocus for the rest of the afternoon. He went home ashamed and more convinced than ever that he could not rely on himself. He says he is tired of living as if the attack is still about to happen, but what frightens him most is the possibility that if he lets his guard down, he will again discover too late that no one is coming to protect anyone and that he will fail in the moment that counts. What he hopes, cautiously, is not to forget, but to stop feeling hunted by something that is over.
